title: Geometrization of continuum mechanics and nonequilibrium thermodynamics: Heat conduction
abstract: We propose a geometric formulation of non-equilibrium heat conduction. It combines the variational (Hamiltonian) structure of symmetric hyperbolic thermodynamically compatible (SHTC) equations with the exterior calculus of differential forms. The central object is the thermal impulse one-form on the four-dimensional matter-time manifold. Its time component is the temperature, and for reversible (ballistic) heat transport it is the exact differential of a scalar potential (i.e. it is holonomic). Non-equilibrium effects are described by a second one-form, the small-scale thermal impulse, which is not required to be exact. Its time component is a fluctuating temperature, and its exterior derivative, the four-thermal vorticity, satisfies a Bianchi-type kinematic identity. The variational principle together with this identity yields a non-equilibrium two-temperature model. Its field equations have the same structure as Maxwell's equations in a medium, with the thermal impulse field, the thermal vorticity field and a thermal Poynting vector contributing to the heat flux. Dissipation is introduced through relaxation terms that conserve the total energy and produce entropy. A formal asymptotic analysis shows that, in the relaxation limit, the model reduces to a Guyer-Krumhansl-type heat conduction with independent transverse and longitudinal length scales. The transverse nonlocal term comes from the spatial non-holonomy of the small-scale thermal impulse, while the longitudinal term comes from its non-holonomy in time, i.e. from the relaxation of the fluctuating temperature. We also discuss the gauge-theoretic interpretation of the model. Its kinematics is that of an abelian gauge theory, while the local gauge symmetry is explicitly broken by the existence of two temperatures. Finally, we discuss the consequences of the geometric structure for structure-preserving numerical methods.
summary: This paper proposes a novel geometric framework for non-equilibrium heat conduction by employing differential forms and variational principles. It constructs a two-temperature model whose field equations mimic those of electromagnetism, providing a mathematically consistent extension beyond classical Fourier theory. The framework successfully recovers known theories like Guyer-Krumhansl while incorporating non-equilibrium effects via geometric terms.
main_problem: To develop a rigorous geometric formulation for non-equilibrium heat conduction that overcomes the limitations of classical Fourier theory.
main_result: The model yields a non-equilibrium two-temperature description whose field equations resemble Maxwell's equations, and it correctly reduces to the Guyer-Krumhansl type theory in the relaxation limit.
method: It combines the variational structure of Symmetric Hyperbolic Thermodynamically Compatible (SHTC) equations with the exterior calculus of differential forms.
model_or_system: The system is heat conduction on a four-dimensional matter-time manifold, modeled using a thermal impulse one-form and a small-scale thermal impulse two-form to capture non-equilibrium effects.
key_observables: Thermal impulse one-form, small-scale thermal impulse, four-thermal vorticity, and the heat flux vector.
important_parameters: Relaxation time ($	au$), transverse and longitudinal length scales, and the two temperatures characterizing the system.
main_assumptions: The theory requires abandoning the local-equilibrium hypothesis and working with hyperbolic PDEs, although it is built upon a variational principle.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the geometric framework, deriving the non-equilibrium two-temperature model with a Maxwell-like structure, demonstrating the recovery of the Guyer-Krumhansl theory in the asymptotic limit, and concluding with discussions on gauge theory and numerical methods.
why_interesting: The rigorous geometric approach to non-equilibrium thermodynamics, particularly the connection between dissipation, curvature, and gauge theory, provides advanced mathematical tools applicable to open quantum systems and non-equilibrium dynamics.
